5eaf464e45df768f: The world’s most important shipping lanes pass through the Strait of Malacca.
Yet, within Malaysia’s maritime boundaries, there is no single framework to determine who gets to use which patch of water and for what purpose.

That shortcoming was the subject of discussion at a recent Ensearch forum “Our Seas, Our Future” where Dr Gopinath Nagaraj and Dr Harinder Rai Singh of FanLi Marine and Consultancy Sdn Bhd (FanLi) made the case for marine spatial planning with a clarity Malaysia would do well to heed.
Their framing of the sea as overlapping estates of biodiversity, fisheries, industry and maritime activity is right. The ocean is not just a shipping lane with some fish in it.
Their point is that fragmented governance, rather than a lack of awareness, is the real barrier.

The numbers bear this out: fisheries production was valued at RM11.43 billion in 2023, Malaysian ports handled more than 30 million TEUs in 2024, and offshore oil, gas and tourism all draw on the same finite waters.
Yet each sector is planned or managed by a different authority under a different law.
Fragmentation is not a natural disaster. It is a choice — the accumulated result of agencies guarding their own turf and a Cabinet unwilling to make one give ground.
The department of environment approves reclamation and coastal EIA reports one environmental impact assessment at a time. That is not enough.

Every silted estuary and buried mudflat in this country may have been approved through a valid EIA. Until the DOE requires cumulative-impact assessments — measuring the combined effect of projects along an entire coastline rather than assessing each project in isolation — its approval process risks certifying decline one project at a time.

The fisheries numbers tell another story. In 2022, marine landings totalled 1.308 million metric tonnes (mt), valued at RM11.3 billion. In 2023, they fell to 1.27 million mt, valued at RM11.43 billion. In 2024, they rose to 1.392 million mt, valued at RM11.84 billion, and in 2025 to 1.393 million mt, valued at RM11.88 billion.

The fisheries department holds the nursery-ground data any marine plan would need. Yet there is still no publicly available national fish-habitat atlas. Food security is its responsibility. Where is the map?
The marine department and the transport ministry plan sea lanes and port expansions as though reefs and fishing grounds simply are not there.
Navigation matters enormously, but it is not the only estate at sea. Too often, the ministry behaves like the senior claimant whose needs are settled before anyone else is consulted.
The malaysian maritime enforcement agency and the navy have the mandate to secure our waters. Yet illegal sand dredging, unpermitted reclamation and foreign incursions continue.
This is the half of the conversation too often forgotten: a marine plan without enforcement is a coloured map. Zoning that no one polices protects nothing.
State governments control the foreshore out to three nautical miles and monetise it through reclamation deals that federal ecological policy struggle to stop.

Every attempt at a “national” ocean policy eventually runs into this constitutional divide. Sabah, Sarawak and reclamation-hungry peninsular states cannot keep hiding behind the Federal Constitution while treating the coastline as an asset to be sold to the highest bidder.
PlanMalaysia (formerly known as the department of town and country planning) and local authorities have been told to extend spatial planning into marine areas.
Yet they lack both the statutory machinery and the planning expertise to do so effectively. Beyond the high-water line, they have done little.
Petronas operates across the same seabed designated for conservation, under terms negotiated federally, without having to reconcile its footprint within an integrated marine plan.
Its data can also become difficult to scrutinise when national security is invoked.
And above all sits the Cabinet. The draft National Ocean Policy, with its proposal for an oceans and fisheries ministry, has remained a draft for years.

This is not a technical shortfall. It is a decision no one has been willing to make because unification means one ministry losing authority to another. That is a failure of political will dressed up as a coordination problem.
The experts who advocated for marine spatial planning (MSP) can only diagnose and recommend.

Their prescription is sound: a national MSP governance unit with a real legal mandate; a marine data system and conflict atlas; pilot planning zones in Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah and Sarawak; and zoning developed through genuine consultation with fisherfolk who actually know the waters. It is the right blueprint.

But blueprints have never been the problem. Malaysia does not lack marine policy; it has too much of it, scattered across a dozen agencies, with none willing to surrender an inch and no single body empowered to force them to work together.
So the test is simple, and it is a test of government, not consultants.
Give one body three things: a legal mandate strong enough to override sectoral silos, a budget line in the next Malaysia Plan, and enforcement teeth on the water.
Most importantly, give it a political structure capable of bringing competing interests together.
The draft National Ocean Policy advocated such an approach. Drawing on a similar challenge faced by Canada, it proposed a ministry of oceans and fisheries.
Anything less, and the next forum will be another well-attended description of a problem we have all agreed on for a decade — held while the reclamation barges keep working just offshore.
The sea is a shared and finite national asset, not empty space reserved for the most powerful claimant. Right now, it has no ministry, no map and no enforcer of its own.
That is not the ocean’s failing. It is ours.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
144e902c5e9c23b3: PETALING JAYA: A good workplace is about more than salary, perks or whether employees enjoy coming to work. Workers also need to understand what is expected of them, see how their contribution matters, and feel they have room to grow without burning themselves out along the way.
With skills gaps, new technologies and changing expectations reshaping the workplace, employers have an increasingly important role in creating jobs that can be sustained over time.
Nicholas Lam, managing director of Jobstreet by SEEK Malaysia, said meaningful work depends on clear expectations, supportive leadership and opportunities to develop.
“When people understand the purpose of their work and have the support to deliver, they are better placed to contribute to their organisation’s growth and their own,” he said.
To that end, here are five ways employers can help build stronger workplaces.
1. Provide work that uses employees' strengths
A good job match starts with understanding the skills a role actually requires and where an employee can make the greatest contribution.

This matters in Malaysia, where 35.2% of employed people with tertiary education were working in semi-skilled or low-skilled occupations in the second quarter of this year, according to the statistics department.

Employers should also help staff understand why their work matters. Someone handling customer queries, for example, should not only know how to resolve individual problems but also how those decisions contribute to better service, and where greater responsibility could eventually lead.
That connection between daily work, business needs and personal growth can make a role feel more purposeful.
2. Make pay progression easier to understand
Competitive pay remains important, but salary satisfaction is not simply about whether employees think they are being paid fairly.
A recent Salary Pulse report found that 81% of Malaysian workers felt fairly or well paid, yet only 49% said they were happy with their salary.
For employers, that suggests pay needs to be considered alongside workload, responsibility and career prospects.

Review criteria should be clear, with employees given a realistic understanding of what they need to demonstrate in order to progress. If budgets are tight, transparency matters too - particularly around what is possible and when the next review may happen.
People are more likely to stay engaged when they can see how growing responsibilities may eventually translate into greater reward.
3. Build performance that can actually be sustained

Employees can enjoy their jobs and still be exhausted by them. One workplace survey found that 70% of Malaysian workers described themselves as happy at work, while 41% also said they felt burnt out or exhausted.
Those figures are not necessarily contradictory. Someone may value their colleagues, enjoy their role - and still struggle with an unsustainable workload.

Managers, therefore, need to look beyond whether people appear happy. Targets should be set with team capacity in mind, priorities should be clear, and regular conversations should include workload and stress rather than focusing solely on results.
If pressure becomes constant, employers may need to reconsider how work is distributed and which tasks genuinely deserve priority.
4. Make flexibility practical, not vague
Flexibility can help more people remain in or return to the workforce, particularly those balancing employment with family responsibilities.
Data from the statistics department from June showed that housework or family responsibilities accounted for 43.3% of people outside the labour force.

Not every job can offer remote work, but flexibility can take different forms. For an office team, it may mean adjustable hours. For staff who need to be onsite, predictable rosters and easier shift swaps can still make a meaningful difference.
The important part is agreeing on outcomes, service coverage and response times while giving employees reasonable autonomy over how they organise their work.
Clear boundaries also matter in connected workplaces, particularly around when staff are expected to be available and when they are free to switch off.
5. Help employees grow alongside technology
Introducing AI or other new technologies is not simply a question of buying new tools: employees need time and guidance to learn how to use them well.

Employers should begin by identifying tasks technology is supposed to improve and what better performance should look like. Staff then need opportunities to practise during working hours, rather than being expected to learn everything on their own time.

It is equally important to explain how roles may change, what new skills will be needed, and where those skills could lead. For younger employees in particular, structured feedback and coaching can help build confidence as well as technical ability.

When learning becomes part of the job rather than an occasional add-on, technology has a better chance of helping people take on more valuable work instead of simply adding another source of pressure.
671a8b121fe3b9ee: PETALING JAYA: Amaran pemimpin PAS Sanusi Nor supaya Umno tidak mempergunakan parti itu mencerminkan dilema lebih besar Umno dalam menentukan hala tuju kerjasama politiknya, kata seorang penganalisis.

Mazlan Ali dari Universiti Teknologi Malaysia (UTM) berkata kenyataan Sanusi menunjukkan sebarang kerjasama antara Umno dan PAS perlu berasaskan rundingan yang jelas serta kedudukan yang diterima kedua-dua pihak.
Pada masa sama, katanya, pendekatan Umno yang berbeza mengikut negeri menunjukkan parti itu masih belum mempunyai formula kerjasama yang seragam, sama ada dengan PAS atau Pakatan Harapan (PH).

Mazlan berkata hubungan BN-PH masih berjalan di peringkat persekutuan serta di negeri seperti Pahang dan Perak, tetapi kedua-dua gabungan mengambil pendekatan berbeza dalam beberapa pilihan raya negeri lain.
“Kita tak dengar desakan daripada Umno Pahang supaya memutuskan hubungan dengan PH. Perak pun sama.
“Menteri besar Pahang dan Perak nampak positif dengan kerjasama itu. Di dua negeri yang diterajui Umno ini, kita tidak nampak krisis yang besar,” katanya kepada FMT.

Pahang ketika ini ditadbir menerusi kerjasama BN-PH, manakala Umno negeri itu turut menilai beberapa kemungkinan jajaran politik termasuk bersama PH, PN atau bertanding secara solo pada pilihan raya akan datang.
Menurut Mazlan, keadaan itu menunjukkan hala tuju kerjasama Umno tidak boleh dilihat melalui satu negeri sahaja kerana pertimbangan politiknya berbeza mengikut keadaan setempat.
Hubungan dengan PAS juga, katanya, masih memerlukan banyak perkara diperincikan sebelum satu bentuk kerjasama lebih menyeluruh dapat diwujudkan.

Sanusi sebelum ini turut mencadangkan rundingan kerusi antara PAS dan Umno dibuat di seluruh negara, bukannya secara berasingan mengikut negeri, bagi memudahkan pelarasan kawasan yang mahu ditandingi kedua-dua parti.
Amaran terbaharu Sanusi timbul ketika parti-parti politik membincangkan kemungkinan kerjasama menjelang PRN Melaka.
Beliau mengingatkan Umno supaya tidak mempergunakannya untuk kepentingan parti itu dan berkata mana-mana pihak yang mahu bekerjasama dengan PAS perlu berunding secara ikhlas tanpa agenda tersembunyi.

Sementara itu, Felo Majlis Profesor Negara Azmi Hassan melihat kenyataan Pengerusi BN Melaka Ab Rauf Yusoh bahawa rundingan kerjasama politik belum bermula sebagai sebahagian daripada strategi tawar-menawar Umno, bukannya petanda PAS cuba dipermainkan.
Menurutnya, ketetapan BN Melaka untuk mempertahankan kerusi yang dimenanginya sebelum ini boleh dijadikan kedudukan awal parti itu dalam sebarang rundingan.
“Jadi itu adalah asas rundingan dan boleh dimaktubkan sebagai dasar atau strategi Umno kepada sesiapa yang ingin berunding atau bekerjasama dengan Umno.
“Mereka perlu menerima kedudukan Umno terlebih dahulu sebelum rundingan boleh bergerak ke peringkat seterusnya,” katanya.
e5962324e76b891a: NEW YORK: Several countries want Malaysia to become a co-chair of the Hague Group alongside South Africa, says foreign minister Mohamad Hasan.
Mohamad attributed the interest to Malaysia’s strong and outspoken position on international platforms.

"This includes the positions expressed by the prime minister, who consistently speaks about violations of international law, violations of international humanitarian law and other issues," he told Malaysian media after delivering the national statement at the 81st United Nations General Assembly here.
However, Mohamad said the matter had yet to be brought to the Cabinet, particularly the prime minister, for approval.

The Hague Group was established in January 2025 by eight countries, including Malaysia and South Africa, to coordinate legal and diplomatic measures in response to violations of international law relating to Palestine.
The group currently lists Colombia and South Africa as its co-chairs, while Malaysia is among its founding members.
It held the Bogota Emergency Conference in July, as well as a high-level meeting at the UN headquarters yesterday.

Mohamad said that groupings such as the Hague Group, Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the Group of 77 were important because they allowed like-minded countries to coordinate their positions, convey them to the UN and follow up on decisions.
"We know that Malaysia is not a major power. Our voice will not carry very far if we stand alone," he said.
"That is why Malaysia joins groups of countries through which we can express our views."
Mohamad also pointed to Asean as another platform through which middle powers could collectively exert greater influence on global issues.
He said the international community was increasingly looking to the 11-member bloc for its position on global crises.
"When Asean speaks, it usually gets support from the international community," he said.
However, Mohamad said Asean had to navigate global issues carefully to avoid being perceived as pursuing particular interests.
He said the bloc should focus on issues such as violations of human rights and international law.
"When such things happen, Asean will speak with the voice of its 11 member states," he said.
f983b71b90f689cf: NEW YORK: Beberapa negara mahu Malaysia menjadi pengerusi bersama Hague Group dengan Afrika Selatan, kata Menteri Luar Mohamad Hasan.
Mohamad berkata cadangan itu timbul susulan pendirian tegas dan lantang Malaysia dalam pelbagai forum antarabangsa.

“Ini termasuk pendirian yang disuarakan perdana menteri, yang secara konsisten membangkitkan mengenai pelanggaran undang-undang antarabangsa, undang-undang kemanusiaan antarabangsa dan isu lain,” katanya kepada media Malaysia selepas menyampaikan kenyataan negara pada Perhimpunan Agung Pertubuhan Bangsa-Bangsa Bersatu (UNGA) ke-81.
Bagaimanapun, Mohamad berkata perkara itu masih belum dibawa kepada Kabinet, khususnya Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim, untuk mendapatkan kelulusan.

Hague Group ditubuhkan pada Januari 2025 oleh lapan negara termasuk Malaysia dan Afrika Selatan bagi menyelaras tindakan undang-undang serta diplomatik dalam menangani pelanggaran undang-undang antarabangsa berkaitan Palestin.
Kumpulan itu kini menyenaraikan Colombia dan Afrika Selatan sebagai pengerusi bersama, manakala Malaysia adalah antara negara pengasas.
Hague Group menganjurkan Persidangan Tergempar Bogota pada Julai lalu dan mengadakan mesyuarat peringkat tinggi di ibu pejabat PBB semalam.

Mohamad berkata kumpulan seperti Hague Group, Pertubuhan Kerjasama Islam (OIC) dan Kumpulan 77 (G77) penting kerana membolehkan negara yang mempunyai pendirian sama menyelaraskan pandangan, menyampaikannya kepada PBB dan membuat susulan terhadap keputusan yang dicapai.
“Kita tahu Malaysia bukan kuasa besar. Jika kita bersendirian, suara kita tidak akan pergi jauh.
“Sebab itu Malaysia menyertai kumpulan negara yang membolehkan kita menyuarakan pandangan bersama,” katanya.
Mohamad turut menyifatkan Asean sebagai satu lagi platform yang membolehkan negara kuasa pertengahan meningkatkan pengaruh secara kolektif dalam menangani isu global.
Katanya, masyarakat antarabangsa kini semakin memberi perhatian kepada pendirian blok 11 negara itu terhadap pelbagai krisis dunia.
“Apabila Asean bersuara, lazimnya ia mendapat sokongan masyarakat antarabangsa,” katanya.
Bagaimanapun, Mohamad berkata Asean perlu berhati-hati dalam menangani isu global supaya tidak dilihat memperjuangkan kepentingan tertentu.
Katanya, blok itu sebaliknya perlu memberi tumpuan kepada isu seperti pelanggaran hak asasi manusia dan undang-undang antarabangsa.
“Apabila perkara seperti itu berlaku, Asean akan bersuara mewakili 11 negara anggotanya,” katanya.
49b16003a1b74d8c: LIVERPOOL: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham declined to give his backing on Sunday to plans to build a third runway at Heathrow, saying it was a matter for people who live near London's main airport.

The government led by his predecessor, former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, announced last year it supported Heathrow's expansion proposal, which must undergo a lengthy planning process before construction can begin.
"I think, principally, it's a matter for London," Burnham told the BBC in an interview at the start of the governing Labour Party's annual conference.
"I think you've got to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation."
Burnham's refusal to immediately back the plan is the latest development in a long-running debate over a project that has divided politicians for two decades.
Heathrow said at the weekend that plans to open the third runway could be delayed by four years, meaning it would not be operational until 2039.

The airport operates at 99% capacity and risks being overtaken in Europe by other airports. Its two runways compare with four each in Paris' Charles de Gaulle and Frankfurt Airport, and six at Amsterdam's Schiphol.

Heathrow is just 24km west of London. Residents have for decades complained about noise pollution, safety risks from flights over the densely populated city, and more recently, about the impact of soaring carbon emissions.
But businesses and workers' unions have raised concern about delays to Heathrow's expansion and the impact on Britain's growth prospects and jobs.
GMB, a union which represents workers across Heathrow, said while local voices should be heard, many were workers who supported expansion and that "this isn't just a matter for London".
"Heathrow is Britain's front door, and businesses in every region trade through it," said Warren Kenny, GMB London regional secretary. "I urge the prime minister to unleash our potential and build."
33492604345cb87b: WASHINGTON: "Avengers: Endgame" dusted competitors in the North American weekend box office, as the 2019 super hero film was re-released in a bid to drum up support for the franchise.
The film holds the title of the second-highest grossing film ever, after earning US$2.8 billion, driven by an ensemble cast including Robert Downey Jr, Josh Brolin and Scarlett Johansson.

Over the weekend, the encore presentation of the Walt Disney film took in US$26 million in North America, for a global total of US$86 million, according to estimates by Exhibitor Relations, a tracking firm.
The re-release comes ahead of the planned Dec 18 debut of "Avenger: Doomsday," with audiences eager to see four new post-credit scenes setting up the forthcoming film.
"As a marketing exercise, it’s an effective way to build early word-of-mouth," said veteran industry watcher David A. Gross.
Taking second place was Sony's "Resident Evil," with an estimated US$23.3 million in North America, for a global total over its first two weeks of over US$196 million.

"Heart of the Beast," starring Brad Pitt as a former soldier and his loyal but traumatised combat dog as they survive in the Alaskan wilderness, brought in an estimated US$20 million on the continent for Paramount on its opening weekend.

Also debuting over the weekend was "Primetime," starring Robert Pattinson as reality TV host Chris Hansen. The film is based on a real-life US show from the mid-2000s called "To Catch a Predator" in which Hansen and his production staff lured would-be pedophiles into sting operations where police were waiting to make on-screen arrests.
The film brought in an estimated US$19.2 million for A24 over the weekend.
"Forgotten Island" an animated family film, however, underperformed over the weekend, bringing in just US$12.8 million for Universal on it's opening weekend.
"This is a weak opening for an original animation film from one of the major labels," Gross said, while noting that reviews were overwhelmingly positive.
Gross expects the film to do well overseas, which should stem some of the losses.

fa5b642b3c5ab5ce: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — Guardhouses, boom gates and security guards have become a familiar sight in residential neighbourhoods across the Klang Valley, but putting them in place is not simply a matter of getting enough neighbours to agree and hiring a security company.

There are rules governing how guarded communities are established, where a guardhouse can be built, when a boom gate can be closed, whether residents can be forced to participate and even where speed bumps can be placed.
And the rules are not exactly the same across Kuala Lumpur and Selangor.
In Kuala Lumpur, City Hall (DBKL) uses the PLANMalaysia guideline as a reference for guarded neighbourhoods.

The four Selangor local authorities Malay Mail is focusing on — Ampang Jaya Municipal Council (MPAJ), Subang Jaya City Council (MBSJ), Shah Alam City Council (MBSA) and Petaling Jaya City Council (MBPJ) — generally follow the Selangor Housing and Property Board (LPHS) framework, with individual councils setting additional requirements according to local conditions.

PLANMalaysia’s 2019 guideline was introduced to guide state and local authorities, technical agencies and residents’ associations in establishing and managing guarded communities in non-strata housing. It replaced the 2010 guideline.

The guideline itself notes that its implementation must be read together with existing laws and other relevant guidelines, and that local authorities can impose conditions according to their respective jurisdictions.
Here is what residents need to know.
1. First, how many residents have to agree?
This is one of the biggest differences.
Under the PLANMalaysia guideline, at least 85 per cent of residents must agree before an application can be made.

The percentage is calculated based on occupied homes. Residents are defined as homeowners or tenants living in the proposed guarded community, while homes that are not continuously occupied are excluded.
In Selangor, the LPHS framework provides for:
75 per cent consent for a guarded community using a manual boom gate; and
100 per cent consent for an automatic boom gate or access-card system.

The Selangor government has confirmed that the LPHS guideline remains the applicable framework, with individual local authorities able to impose more detailed requirements according to their respective areas and circumstances.
For DBKL, the current publicly cited requirement is at least 81 per cent consent for a guarded neighbourhood scheme, while automatic boom gates using facial recognition require 100 per cent consent.
So a neighbourhood does not necessarily need unanimous support simply to establish a guarded community.
But it is a different story if residents want an automatic access system.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Boom gates controlling vehicle access at a guarded residential area. Guidelines differ depending on whether access is manual or automated. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
2. Getting the required percentage does not mean residents can be forced to join
This is an important protection for residents who disagree.
The PLANMalaysia guideline says the process of obtaining consent must not involve coercion or pressure on residents who do not agree.
The Selangor framework likewise states that there should be no coercion to join the scheme.
So if a neighbourhood reaches the required threshold, that does not mean every resident has automatically agreed to participate.
3. A resident who does not join cannot be locked out
This is perhaps the most important practical rule.
The PLANMalaysia guideline states that residents who do not participate in the scheme cannot be prevented from entering their homes at any time.
That means a resident who refuses to join cannot be denied access to his or her home merely for not participating in the scheme.
The Selangor guidelines contain the same basic principle.
4. A boom gate cannot simply be used to block access
The guidelines also prohibit vehicles from being obstructed when entering or leaving the neighbourhood.
This is significant because a guarded community does not automatically turn a public residential road into a private one.

PLANMalaysia’s guideline requires the scheme to have access arrangements that do not obstruct traffic, while its management conditions state that public authorities and members of the public must be allowed to enter and use public roads and facilities.
The Selangor guidelines similarly prohibit guards from denying lawful access to residents, members of the public and authorities.
This does not prevent an approved guarded scheme from operating security procedures at its entrance, but those arrangements cannot be used to bar people who are entitled to enter.
5. The boom gate is generally supposed to operate only from midnight to 6am
Under the PLANMalaysia guideline, a boom gate is generally allowed to operate from midnight to 6am.
A local authority may consider allowing it to remain closed 24 hours a day, but only if security guards are stationed there around the clock and can open the barrier whenever necessary.
This means a neighbourhood cannot simply install a boom gate and keep it permanently closed because residents prefer tighter access control.
6. Automatic access systems are a different matter
The PLANMalaysia guideline says automatic access cards can only be allowed if 100 per cent of residents agree.
Selangor’s LPHS framework similarly sets 100 per cent consent for automatic boom gates or access-card systems.
The Selangor government has said the higher threshold is intended to protect residents’ rights and avoid disputes over access between participating and non-participating households.
This contrasts with manual boom gates, for which the Selangor framework sets a 75 per cent consent threshold.
7. An automatic system does not necessarily mean one lane for everyone
This is where individual council rules become more detailed.

MBPJ’s guidelines allow an access-card arrangement to be considered with two separate lanes — one for residents and another for visitors — provided there are 24-hour guards and the other MBPJ conditions are met.
MPAJ also has requirements governing arrangements for residents and visitors when considering automated access systems.

So while the basic PLANMalaysia guideline does not prescribe a universal “resident lane” and “visitor lane” for every guarded community, individual councils may set more detailed conditions when automatic access is proposed.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A security guard attends to a motorist at the entrance to a guarded residential neighbourhood. Guarded-community schemes remain subject to local authority rules on access and security procedures. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin
8. There are even rules on where speed bumps can go
This is another detail many residents may not know.
PLANMalaysia allows speed breakers or road humps to be installed before and after the guardhouse.
But the guideline does not give residents a free hand to put them wherever they want. They must comply with specifications issued by the relevant local authority.
MBSA, for example, gives specific dimensions based on road width.
Its guideline states that for a 50ft road, the road hump should be 5ft wide, while for a 66ft road, it should be 10ft wide.
So even something as seemingly simple as a speed bump outside a guardhouse is subject to council requirements.
9. The guardhouse itself cannot just be built anywhere
PLANMalaysia says the guardhouse should be located on the road shoulder and must not obstruct traffic.
It cannot be built on or in the middle of the road under the national guideline.
The guideline also says the guardhouse cannot be built until the relevant temporary construction permit or approval has been obtained.
The national guideline specifies a maximum size of 1.8m by 2.4m, although Selangor councils have their own specifications.
For example, MPAJ, MBSJ and MBPJ generally use a 6ft by 8ft specification, while MBSA has different dimensions depending on whether a toilet is included.
10. A permanent guardhouse needs another layer of approval

If a guardhouse occupies the road shoulder and is a permanent structure, the residents’ association may need a Temporary Occupation Licence (TOL) from the District and Land Office under Section 65 of the National Land Code 1965.
The PLANMalaysia guideline also requires the guardhouse location to be shown on plans submitted to the relevant land office and local authority.
So a residents’ association cannot simply construct a permanent guardhouse on the road reserve because residents have voted for it.
11. There should be at least two access routes for emergencies
PLANMalaysia’s technical requirements say a guarded community should have at least two entry and exit routes for emergency purposes.
This is separate from the question of whether there is a residents’ lane and a visitors’ lane.
The requirement is about ensuring sufficient access in an emergency, rather than simply creating a convenient arrangement for residents and visitors.
12. Entrance gateways may require separate approval
The PLANMalaysia guideline restricts structures that span or obstruct the entrance road as part of a guarded-neighbourhood scheme.
However, individual councils may have their own procedures for considering entrance gateways.
MBPJ, for example, allows applications for entrance gateways to be considered separately through the planning-permission process, subject to the necessary technical approvals.
So residents should not assume that approval for a guarded-community scheme automatically allows them to build a large gateway or arch over the entrance road.
13. You cannot simply build a wall around the neighbourhood
0619979f92a62bea: KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 28 — Food science nutritionist Yap Ke Yee established Notti Sdn Bhd in July 2023 to address a personal lack of nutritious pet food options in the market.

Finding pet food with the nutritional value she wanted for her dog and two cats was not easy, but Yap turned that hindrance into a business opportunity by developing premium pet food brand Notti Pet Food.

Today, the company is targeting exports to account for at least 50 per cent of its sales within three years, up from about 10 per cent currently, as it expands in Southeast Asia and builds a Malaysian brand for international markets.
Yap said her experience as a pet owner, combined with her food science background, led her to identify a gap in Malaysia’s pet food market, particularly in nutritional options.
“Before starting the business, my research found that nutritionally wise options for pet food are lacking in the industry, and no one is doing anything about it.
“It was challenging to find a pet food brand that uses ingredients high in nutrition, especially kibbles,” she told Bernama.
That frustration became the foundation for Notti, which aims to raise pet nutrition standards through fresh meat, functional recipes and different production technologies.

From a team of four, the company has grown to 10 employees and now offers about 40 stock-keeping units, ranging from slow-baked kibbles to treats, supplements and pet accessories under its Notti Living line.
Yap emphasised that all of Notti’s cat food kibbles are suci-certified by the Islamic Food Research Centre (Hong Kong).
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Notti offers about 40 products, ranging from slow-baked kibble and treats to supplements and pet accessories. — Bernama pic
Growth through challenges
As Notti grew, Yap faced repeated stock shortages, putting pressure on cash flow and inventory.
“We had an out-of-stock major crisis a couple of times,” she said.
Notti subsequently secured US$500,000 (RM2.4 million) in seed funding from 500 South-east Asia and First Move, backed by Khazanah Nasional Bhd via Dana Impak and Jelawang Capital.
Yap said the funding improved inventory management and cash flow, while investors provided guidance, contacts and ideas to move the business forward.
She is also mindful of keeping premium pet food accessible to pet owners facing cost issues.

Notti’s “Crunchy Baked” range combines slow-baked and commercial production technologies to offer larger packaging at a more affordable price point, while maintaining its focus on nutrition and quality ingredients.

“We realise that we need to cater to different price points. Although it uses slightly lower fresh meat content, we still maintain our core focus on pet nutrition and high-quality ingredients for the recipes,” said Yap.
Notti is also set to launch its first wet cat food line next month, with two formats and four flavours, following high demand.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Notti founder Yap Ke Yee said the company aims for exports to account for at least half of sales within three years. — Bernama pic

To mitigate rising raw material and logistics costs, the company prioritises cost-effective organic marketing, leveraging social media platforms rather than heavy advertising expenditure to maintain financial efficiency.
Notti also regularly organises activities with pet owners, building a community beyond selling pet food.
From Malaysia to regional expansion
Yap believes that her close connection with pet owners is also shaping Notti’s regional expansion.
The company is eyeing Indonesia and Vietnam as its next markets, while expanding its presence in Malaysia, where it has about 250 retail touchpoints.
Notti is already present in Singapore, Brunei, the Philippines and Macau, with about 30 overseas touchpoints, as well as on Amazon in the United States.
Rather than simply placing products on shelves, Yap said Notti wants to work with local distributors to build the brand in new markets.

She also hopes to bring the latest pet food manufacturing technologies to Malaysia to benefit the industry. Yap said the technology needed to produce Notti’s fresh-meat kibble is not available in Malaysia, although she sees potential for local manufacturing as demand grows.
“We are ready to represent Malaysia not just from the ingredients, but from the packaging as well. We want to represent the country as a nutritious Malaysian pet food brand,” she said. — Bernama
27d02fff54aeb928: BENGALURU, Sept 28 — The demolition has begun at Bengaluru’s Urvashi Cinema, once a 1,200-seat movie palace where generations of filmgoers cheered and whistled, another casualty of India’s vanishing single-screen era.
“The theatre came up in the 1970s... I was so happy when it opened,” said Manjunath, watching as seats were ripped out and strewn outside.
Manjunath, who uses one name, recalled its glory days, when the shop he runs opposite was packed with customers buying snacks before and after shows.
“That was the rush... now I have a lot of free time,” he said. “But what to do? There is barely any crowd.”
The peeling facades, faded signs and cavernous auditoriums of such cinemas are remnants of a time when going to the movies was itself the main event.

“It is a completely different experience,” said photographer Hemant Chaturvedi, 58, who has documented what remains during a seven-year odyssey, photographing 1,350 single-screen cinemas across 1,000 towns.

His photographs capture not only the movie houses but their ornate facades and decay — a record of a cultural landscape disappearing as cinemas are demolished, converted into multiplexes or left to crumble.
‘Ecosystem is fading’
“People would be cheering, jumping on the seats, even throwing money at the screen,” Chaturvedi said.
The old halls offered a collective, interactive experience, with fans applauding at the hero’s entrance, clapping to romantic songs and shouting at dramatic twists.
“Now that old ecosystem is fading, and the charm is being lost,” he said.
India’s single-screen cinemas have been steadily squeezed by multiplexes, streaming, rising property costs and the expense of maintaining ageing buildings and equipment.
Researchers estimate that India had around 14,000 single-screen halls in the 1980s. Only around 2,000 remain today.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
People watch the early morning show of the newly released Kannada film ‘Toxic’ at the single-screen Mukunda Theatre in Bengaluru August 26, 2026. — AFP pic
Many of the old halls could accommodate around 1,000 people, creating a communal atmosphere rarely found in today’s multiplexes.
The decline has also changed the way Indians experience films. New halls offer air conditioning, reclining seats and food delivered to the seat.
“To me, the new cinemas have lost the charm,” said Chaturvedi, a former Bollywood cinematographer who worked on hit movies during a three-decade career.
“The multiplexes are a generic, cold experience.”
‘Old times’
Some of the old cinemas have been restored and renovated, and the single-screen experience still has its devotees.
In Bengaluru, Mukunda Cinemas still draws crowds — even for early-morning shows before work.
Hundreds lined up before dawn for a recent 6:00 am screening of the latest release of film star Yash, who is hugely popular in India’s Kannada-language cinema.
Santosh, a 47-year-old businessman who uses one name, queued with hundreds of others as crowds set off fireworks outside while waiting for the show.

“Only in the single screen theatres can they take the cinema to the next level, it increases the tradition of cinema,” Santosh said, as cheers and whistles reverberated through the packed hall before the film began.
Veerain Reddy, the third generation of his family running the 50-year-old theatre, said maintaining the establishment “was not an easy task”.
Inflation, rising costs and “so much competition” have made business tough.
“But people who are really passionate are still trying to maintain these single-screen theatres, where people come to watch and celebrate cinema,” he told AFP.
Another survivor in Mumbai — formerly known as Bombay — is the Regal Cinema, an Art Deco hall that opened in 1933.
“The rest of them feel very artificial, commercial, very blingy,” said 23-year-old fan Vanshika. “But Bombay has little places which remind us of the old times.” — AFP
b181a98c8263812e: KHARTOUM, Sept 28 — They came home to a war-ruined city determined to rebuild their lives, but a chronic lack of power, water, jobs and medicine has left many residents of Sudan’s capital wishing they had stayed away.
About four million people fled Khartoum after war broke out between the army and a paramilitary force in 2023, in fighting that reduced large parts of the city to rubble.
But the estimated 2.7 million who have returned since the army recaptured Khartoum last year are caught between joy at being home and the harsh realities of living there.
Businessman Emad Khaled said he was sending his family back to Egypt, while he remains in Khartoum for his work.
“Bringing my family back was a mistake,” the 43-year-old told AFP near the city centre, which is filled with blackened, bombed-out buildings.
Multiple government officials, ordered back to Khartoum, told AFP they were also leaving their families outside the country.
Fighting between the armed forces and paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) is still raging elsewhere in Sudan, including in the Darfur, Kordofan and Blue Nile regions.
The army, strongly encouraging Khartoum’s residents to return, rebuilt the airport and reopened it for domestic flights, and patched up infrastructure.
However, electricity and water still go out for days at a time. And while markets across the capital are open again, many people are unemployed and have little money to spend.
‘Price goes up every day’
By June, only one percent of Khartoum had been declared safe by the UN, with dozens of children killed and injured by booby-traps and unexploded shells lurking within walls and on street corners.
Nearly half a million people have returned from neighbouring Egypt, where 1.5 million Sudanese sought shelter but faced soaring living costs, racial persecution, arrests and deportations.
Khartoum’s working-class neighbourhoods have seen the highest numbers of returnees, while most of those who can afford to stay away.

Consequently, upscale districts such as Khartoum 2 lie abandoned. Along tree-lined avenues, glass crackles underfoot and only birdsong fills the air between empty villas, entire corners of them blown out by missiles.
Thuraya Babiker, 86, thought she had returned for good. But three months later, “my husband, my youngest daughter and I are leaving for the United Arab Emirates”, she told AFP.
“We don’t want to leave,” she said, explaining that the lack of medical care makes it impossible to stay.
As people started returning last year, Sudanese charities rushed to rebuild hospitals, some of which are now “better than before”, health workers say.
But despite their best efforts, physician Haifa Omar says “some things just aren’t available”.
“We have to ask patients to buy some medicines on their own dime. I have a lump in my throat as I say it, we know how difficult people’s situations are.”
College professor Imam Babiker has to visit 10 pharmacies to find his father’s blood pressure medication, “and every day it’s a different price”, he said.
The 34-year-old bought a refrigerator to store his diabetic mother’s insulin, “but the electricity goes out for 12 hours a day, so it gets ruined,” he told AFP.
Others like Souad Mohamed, 49, had her fridge stolen by looters and couldn’t afford a replacement.
“So now I have to buy vegetables and meat every day, and the price goes up every day,” she said.
‘Things really aren’t fine’
Khartoum, once a major African capital home to more than eight million people, is a shell of its former self.
In the city centre, a veteran UN official told AFP the level of destruction dwarfs every other crisis they had seen, including Ukraine.
Although occasional RSF drone strikes continue, Khartoum’s university students have been told they must return, after authorities ended remote learning in July.
Khartoum University medical professors have threatened to resign en masse in protests, while students complain they are being forced back.

“The university’s refusing to let me defend my thesis online, even though my supervisor is also in a different country and doesn’t want to return,” one master’s student told AFP, requesting anonymity.

An undergraduate management student, who should be starting her senior year, said she missed in-person exams this summer and is now scrambling for scholarships in Egypt to restart college from scratch.
“They wouldn’t listen to us, all they cared about was for people to return,” she told AFP.
“To me it’s political, they want people back to show that things are fine, when things really aren’t fine.” — AFP
d2d3ffd0a0098128: KATHMANDU, Sept 28 — Nepal’s hydropower boom has long been touted as a cornerstone of economic growth and renewable energy, but the devastating flood in August exposed its vulnerability.

The disaster triggered by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing — while knocking 410 megawatts (MW), or about 10 per cent of the generation capacity, out of Nepal’s power system.

More than 90 per cent of Nepal’s electricity comes from hydropower, but extensive damage to its river projects has prompted questions about its energy security as climate and geological risks intensify.

“Hydropower has been a major driving force in growth of the country... generating jobs and income,” Uttam Bhlon Lama, senior vice president of the Independent Power Producers’ Association (IPPAN), told AFP.
“It was bringing huge hope and future prospects to the people,” he said, adding that the country would now have to rethink its dam-building spree.
“We have to prepare... This is our new normal.”

Over the past decade, the Himalayan nation has increased hydropower output more than fourfold to about 4,120 megawatts, according to government figures, helping connect nearly all its 30 million people to the grid.

The country had previously moved to export surplus electricity to neighbouring India and Bangladesh, seeking to turn its glacier-fed rivers into a source of revenue. Authorities suspended electricity exports after the disaster.

The major destruction of hydropower infrastructure underscored the risks of that strategy in a region where glaciers are retreating, permafrost is thawing and extreme hazards are becoming harder to predict.
‘Serious lessons’
Nepal’s energy sector accounted for about half of the infrastructure damage from the disaster, according to government assessments.
Seven hydropower projects were directly hit while generation was halted at others, removing 410 MW from the national grid.
Six hydropower projects under construction, with a combined capacity of 508 MW, were also damaged.
Rescuers have continued searching hydropower tunnels for hundreds of missing workers, engineers and other personnel, weeks after the disaster.
The scale of the damage has prompted calls for a rethink of how projects are designed and built.
The disaster has “taught us serious lessons for the future”, Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha told parliament on Wednesday.
“We must not only take stock of the damage but also learn from it and develop systems to reduce future risks,” he said.
The World Bank warned that Nepal needs to build a hydropower system capable of anticipating, absorbing and recovering from increasingly complex Himalayan hazards.
Scientists say the August disaster was caused by a complex chain of geological and climatic factors rather than a single extreme weather event.
According to the World Weather Attribution group, the massive rock-and-ice collapse was shaped by long-term warming, glacier retreat and geological instability.
‘Existential threat’
Much of Nepal’s hydropower infrastructure lies along steep river valleys fed by glaciers — terrain exposed to floods, landslides and cascading geological hazards.
“Powerhouses need to be moved higher up from the riverbeds to protect them against floods, we need better evacuation plans and stocked safehouses,” IPPAN’s Lama said.
“We should explore remotely operated systems so people are not stuck inside in case anything happens.”
The flooding has also renewed calls for diversifying the power mix in Nepal, which lacks coal or gas-fired generation capacity.

“Nepal’s electricity system, currently strained and heavily dependent on hydropower, could be made more robust through well-planned additions of solar electricity,” Germany’s development agency GIZ said in a 2024 report.
The challenge extends beyond Nepal.

Glaciers in the wider Himalayan and Hindu Kush ranges are a crucial water source for around 240 million people in the mountainous regions, as well as for another 1.65 billion people in the South Asian and Southeast Asian river valleys below.
Basanta Raj Adhikari, director at the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribhuvan University, said the Himalayas must be monitored regionally for hotspots to develop early warning systems.
“I call it the fate of the Himalayan people,” he told AFP.
“It can happen anywhere in the world but the Himalayas are experiencing adverse impacts due to climate change and anthropogenic activity,” he said.
“We have to design climate-resilient infrastructures. That is our top priority because we are (facing) existential threat.” — AFP
ce70dbb38957bdd7: I saw a social media post about a man so old he’s bent double but still doing motorcycle food delivery. Most comments on the post were positive and laudatory, seeing this as evidence that, in spite of advanced age, some people still want to be useful and be seen as “normal”.
Yeah, as normal as old people in developed countries working as cashiers at convenience stores or cleaning tables at fast-food joints.
I don’t buy that. If somebody of that age and physical condition is still running around delivering food, they aren’t doing it for fun or for the flex.

I'm a retiree. I’m not rich but I think I have “enough”, whatever enough is. It could turn out I don’t actually have enough and will end my days burdening others or, just as bad in my view, that I have more than enough -- which means I’ve wasted too much of my life acquiring wealth and not actually living it.

May I be spared these two calamities. I’m more inclined to believe that not having enough is the real reason the old bent-double man still runs around doing food deliveries. He’s not doing it for the fresh air or to meet new people.

And may you be spared that fate, too. Life gets tougher every day and not a single day passes that I don’t think about my good fortune of having retired and being able to approach 70 in relatively good physical and economic health. I also can’t help but think of those worse off than me every single day.

In the old days people didn’t really retire. They just stopped working when their body couldn’t handle it any more or when their grown-up children started taking care of them. Those who had actual pensions, mostly retired government employees, were the extra lucky ones.

I chose to retire in my early 60s with a year of my employment contract still to run. Things were changing at my employer's - the usual corporate transformation stuff - and it was best I left and let the new bosses choose my replacement themselves.

In effect I had a year-long pre-retirement leave: I have nothing to complain about and plenty to be grateful for. But some of my corporate peers chose to continue working, and I doubt it’s because they need the money. I surmise they need the job as a validation of some sorts – that 'Hey, I'm still needed and relevant and important'!

I don’t miss the good old corporate warrior days. What I do miss is the interaction with people at work, which I replace by making new friends while still keeping the old ones. Many still remember me and I never say no to a chance for a free meal and listen to them whinge about their bosses!

Through my career, I never took myself seriously. I earned enough to live a comfortable life and feed and clothe and educate my kids. My four decades of being a pen-pusher also gave me “enough” for my retirement, which I think is what running the rat race should be about.

Malaysia is still a country of young people but as lifespans increase there are an increasing number of people like me, comfortably retired and with years still ahead of us. But there are also many others like that old man who, allegedly, still does motorcycle delivery in spite of his advanced age and medical condition.

Having “enough” helps you be independent. There is life outside of work and that spared me the pain of leaving my title, office, and other perks behind. After all I wasn’t teaching the young or curing the sick or growing food or keeping society safe through unglamorous jobs as firemen or rubbish collectors. What I did for a living wasn’t really fundamental to the survival of our species.

Many middle-aged people, especially government servants, pray for an optional early retirement that can't come early enough. They’re probably stuck in a toxic work environment just to put food on the table and perhaps squirrel away some money for retirement. That’s not living - that’s just surviving.

That we’re a country of many young people still toiling away to create wealth for themselves, and hence for the country, is a blessing. Their labour ensures that our pension funds and investments and social safety nets such as public healthcare will still last at least for a few more decades.

However, the younger generation are not guaranteed a safety net and soft landing when they retire. We post-WW2 “Baby Boomers” are the wealthiest generation ever, but we may need that wealth to take care of ourselves and not burden our own children, whose own wealth and filial piety may not be enough to care for us.

Our generation’s wealth also unfortunately comes from destructive greed. We live a better life than our parents but the price of our good life comes from ruining the climate and depleting and defiling the earth’s resources and creating economic and social disparities. Such is the world we’re handing to our kids.

Apart from relationships and independence, health matters more as we age. We once traded our time and even health to make money. Now, we’re trying to trade money for time and health. But time and health are elusive and without some humility in our life perspectives, they still can’t guarantee a peaceful autumn of our life.

Ironically a solution for a happier final chapter perhaps lies in giving back to others. When I recall the old Japanese rescue workers at the Fukushima nuclear plant disaster as well as the elderly British protesters against the Gaza genocide who volunteered to be arrested in the UK, I choke up.

These brave old people purposely chose harm and danger for themselves to protect those younger than themselves. They had a good innings in the game of life, and are now willing to sacrifice to help the younger ones play their own innings. It’s the ultimate measure of having lived a good life that you’re prepared to lose it to protect others.

I’m extremely lucky I never had to make such a decision, or even have to be on a motorcycle to deliver food. I’d like to think I’d have discharged myself honourably if tested. But I’m in no hurry to put myself to these tests!

e6adf117654cb8c3: Benighted politics are once again haunting the Balkans. This month’s semi-official funeral in Belgrade for the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić, whom many Bosnian Serbs still honour, has dredged up past traumas and reignited nationalist tensions. Diplomatic relations between Serbia and Bosnia are deteriorating, casting further doubt on Serbia’s already semi-stalled accession to the European Union.

Worse, while Europe and the US used to be mostly aligned in their support for the tenuous political process in Bosnia, that is no longer the case. Whereas previous US presidents might have been accused of being overly interventionist, Donald Trump’s administration has shown no interest in the region’s delicate political processes whatsoever. Its sole concern is to advance narrow economic interests, and this has meant tolerating or even supporting hardline Serbian nationalists in Bosnia.

For example, the Trump administration has thrown its support behind a gas pipeline that would connect the Croatian coast to Sarajevo (the Bosnian capital). At first glance, such a project makes sense, given its potential to alleviate the region’s dependence on Russian gas. But when contracts may suspiciously be awarded to a previously unknown company whose leaders have “personal connections to Donald Trump,” warning lights start flashing.

Warning lights are flashing on the political front, too. Bosnia will hold elections this October, and depending on the outcome, hardline Serb forces may join with hardline Croats to change the country’s governance framework. The timing for such a gambit is ideal because the US obviously would look the other way. But should it succeed, the Bosniak (Muslim) community is bound to feel threatened and will respond accordingly. That would increase the risk of a downward spiral that could profoundly destabilise the country.

Moreover, Serbia will also hold elections in October. After years of mass student protests, the government is facing a broad grassroots opposition movement, which is now organised under the banner of the “Student List”. With the outcome still far from certain, one can easily imagine a scenario in which President Aleksandar Vučić’s populist regime simply declares victory, triggering even more instability.

The situation in Kosovo is no calmer. Reconciliation talks between Serbia and Kosovo have stalled, and local authorities in the divided town of Mitrovica have yet to be given responsibility for the bridge linking the Serbian and Albanian districts, owing to fears of what might follow.

More broadly, the country’s political system is deadlocked, and anger over the Kosovo Specialist Chambers’ recent conviction of Hashim Thaci, a former military leader who served as president of Kosovo from 2016 to 2020, has further alienated the country from its previous international partners.

None of these developments would necessarily be destabilising on its own. But taken together, they risk creating a critical mass of nationalist sentiment. The central idea behind the peace processes a quarter-century ago was that a combination of EU accession talks and reconciliation facilitated by various international tribunals would gradually bring stability and cooperation to the region. But that hope has not been vindicated.

With the exception of Montenegro, and possibly Albania, integration into the EU has stalled and lost much of its power as a motivating force. Equally disappointing, the proceedings led by international tribunals at The Hague have been so grotesquely drawn out as to have no chance of promoting reconciliation. They may even be making the situation worse.

Tiny Montenegro is still on a promising trajectory, but whether its EU accession bid could survive a new whirlwind of regional turmoil is far from certain. If Serbia has an interest in destabilising its neighbour, it can easily do so.

As is always the case in the Balkans, there are no easy solutions to address the rising tensions. Each country has its own political processes, but the risk of mutually reinforcing spillovers is high. With the US focussed solely on private economic interests, and with the EU distracted by Russian aggression and US unpredictability, the prospects for coherent international policies to restore stability, promote reconciliation, and support integration are bleak.

This doesn’t mean we are heading towards a new round of Balkan wars. But even limited skirmishes could be sufficient to push the entire region onto a more uncertain and dangerous path. Political leaders, particularly in Europe, must heed the alarm. The Balkans brought major wars to Europe twice in the previous century, and they could easily create instability in this century, too.
Carl Bildt is a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden.

914bb2017c706e9d: Thirty years after Apple abandoned Copland, its doomed attempt to create a modern Mac operating system, a new emulator lets you try the final developer build in your browser. Copland was intended to replace Apple's System 7 with a PowerPC-native operating system built around a microkernel, protected memory, and preemptive multitasking for system services. Three unfinished developer builds – D7E1, D9, and D11E4 – are publicly known. Relatively few people outside Apple's developer community in the mid-1990s ever had the opportunity to use them. Now you can boot Apple Copland D11E4 in your browser and explore the unstable prerelease OS without installing anything. Developer Michael Steil, also known as Mist, made it possible with an experimental fork of the DingusPPC Power Mac emulator. Steil says the 11 patches that enable DingusPPC to boot Copland were written with AI assistance. The upstream project does not accept AI-assisted patches, so the fixes would have to be rewritten before they could be incorporated. Don't expect miracles. The emulator runs D11E4, the final build Apple distributed to developers, dating from June 1996. It remains very much unfinished: if the emulated system hits an assertion, it drops into a debugger and asks the user to continue manually. Apple CEO Gil Amelio had demonstrated Copland at the company's 1995 Worldwide Developers Conference, but the project never approached the stability required for release. Much of Copland existed as plans and documentation rather than finished code. In 2009, Steil assembled an extensive archive of that material in Apple Copland Reference Documentation. There was also a planned successor to Copland, codenamed Gershwin, but it remained nothing more than a plan. The modern Gershwin desktop we covered a year ago is a nod to that nonexistent OS. Anyone familiar with the classic Mac OS of the late 1990s will recognize parts of Copland, and for good reason. Copland overran so badly that Amelio recruited the late Ellen Hancock from IBM as Apple's chief technology officer and tasked her with getting the project back on track. After reviewing its progress, she instead recommended cancelling it and acquiring an operating system elsewhere. Apple considered several alternatives, including acquiring Be for BeOS and working with Sun on a system based on Solaris. It ultimately bought NeXT, bringing Steve Jobs back to the company along with NeXTSTEP. Hancock was later sidelined under Jobs and resigned in 1997. Apple acquired NeXT at the end of 1996, just months after cancelling Copland. The first developer release of its NeXTSTEP-based successor, Rhapsody, followed in 1997 – continuing the musical codenames, if not the code. Rhapsody evolved into Mac OS X Server 1.0 in 1999 and the consumer release of Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001. Replacing the Mac OS architecture took years. While that work continued, Apple folded some of Copland's more mature components into updates to its existing operating system. Mac OS 8, released in 1997, gained Copland's Platinum interface and a PowerPC-native, multithreaded Finder. Its Appearance control panel supported themes, although Apple shipped only Platinum. Renaming what had been planned as Mac OS 7.7 also helped Apple end the clone program, whose licensing agreements covered System 7. Mac OS 8.1 followed in 1998 with HFS+, Apple's new format for larger disks. Later that year, Mac OS 8.5 became the first PowerPC-only release. Further pieces of Copland's work appeared across Mac OS 8 and 9, allowing Apple to improve the old platform while Mac OS X was being prepared. When Apple bought NeXT, NeXTSTEP already ran on Motorola 680x0, Intel x86, Sun SPARC and HP PA-RISC processors. That portable foundation later helped Apple move the Mac to Intel, while OS X became the basis for the operating systems used by the iPhone and iPad. Apple's future might have looked very different had Copland succeeded. Now it's easier than ever to see why it didn't. ®
d2dfe33bda6046d1: Big AI has a problem. Its companies must ingest other people’s work. You know, books, news stories, photographs, code, websites, that one original meme you came up with, and practically everything else on the internet to train its large language models (LLMs). We all know that. We also know that AI companies hate paying for any of it, obeying the licenses attached to it, or, God forbid, sharing their revenue with the companies and people who created the work in the first place. Recently, Big AI's default way of doing business: "Take it now, argue about legality later," has become more in your face than ever. Look, for example, at the copyright fight between The New York Times and OpenAI and Microsoft. According to 404 Media’s reporting on recently unsealed court documents - arguments from the plaintiffs that the court has not yet ruled on - Microsoft allegedly knew what it was doing when it was importing the internet willy-nilly. Microsoft's Director of Applied Science, Dr. Brent Hecht, was quoted in the news plaintiffs' 92-page combined brief as saying: the case was about “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions." Indeed, it was possibly the “largest theft of labor in human history,” he was quoted as saying in the summary judgment brief from the journalists' lawyers [PDF].This, mind you, wasn't a comment by a member of the press; it was from a senior Microsoft staffer. Hecht wasn't the only one at Microsoft who commented. In an internal Microsoft policy document also quoted in the court papers, the authors admitted generative AI could “significantly disrupt the employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained [because] LLMs are a product that destroys its supply chain.” That, in turn, leads to model collapse. Ironically, AI is killing the content-creator goose that lays the gold eggs of worthwhile content. Judge Sidney H. Stein of the US District Court for the Southern District of New York has not yet issued a decision on the case. OpenAI and Microsoft are actively disputing the plaintiffs' allegations under a "fair use" defense. They contend that using public articles and books to train large language models helps push forward public knowledge, and isn't acting as a "unlawful economic market substitute". But the statements the documents cites are real. Big AI knows it needs the content. Some of the companies concerned don't give a damn; money now, worry later is their motto. Those who can look past the revenue numbers are well aware they're engaged in what Microsoft itself called a “doom loop” of AI content strategy in those unsealed court documents. Will that stop them? Nah. According to the filing [PDF], which refers to sworn deposition testimony of OpenAI’s own corporate representative, it also testified that its LLMs were happy to vacuum up other people's work even when a paywall nominally protected it. Its rep was quoted as saying they were unaware of “any effort to detect paywall content in its training datasets” or “to remove paywall content from its training datasets.” When OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman was told OpenAI could hack its way through the firewall, he responded, “ah, nice.” Whether or not these statements are found to be reflective of a wider attitude, similar attitudes prevail amongst Big AI. Such policies could eventually come back and bite the LLM makers; it's already affecting the market for journalism, fiction writing, graphics creation, anything that demands humans actually get paid for producing original work. But Big AI just doesn't want to pay for it. That's not a side effect. It's the business model. Joe User couldn't care less. They just want a quick answer that sounds right. Some of them couldn't care less about getting the right answers. As for looking deeper to see if the information they're regurgitating is accurate, forget about it! As an OpenAI software engineer put it: “No matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.” Well, I click. That's a big reason why Perplexity is my AI of choice. It's not that it gives a more reliable answer. No, it's that, unlike most LLMs, Perplexity provides sources and links, and I check them before accepting what it tells me. But then I'm a journalist whose degrees are in history, where my professors drummed into me that you always - always - look at the primary sources. Big AI takes the same approach with its code generators. The US Ninth Circuit recently handed GitHub, Microsoft, and OpenAI a narrow win in the Doe v. GitHub lawsuit. The court ruled that the plaintiffs hadn't established a claim under one particular provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), which concerns the removal or alteration of copyright-management information (CMI). In short, the court said that generating new code without including CMI is not necessarily the same thing as removing or altering copyright information from an existing work. Judge Eric Miller wrote: “One who creates a new work and fails to include CMI cannot be said to have ‘removed’ or ‘altered’ anything.” This ruling didn't establish that GitHub Copilot or any other coding model may train on every open source project without restriction. It didn't determine that copying source code into a training set is always fair use. It did not decide that generated code cannot infringe copyright. And it certainly did not repeal the GPL, Apache, BSD, MIT, or any other open-source license. After all, open source isn't a synonym for “do whatever you want with it.” It just seems that way when AI gets its hands on open source code. That's the problem with AI-generated code. A programmer who receives a Copilot suggestion is very unlikely to check whether the GPL covers the code, or whether Apache covers the snippet from a library. The developer certainly can't tell which license terms may apply to the code that just popped up from Opus 5.5 or GPT 6. As the guy from OpenAI said, people don't click the links, and in AI-enabled programming pipelines, they don't even have the links anyway. An open source-savvy attorney friend of mine has a bigger worry than this narrow decision. He told me that what gives him "pause is a broader trend. There are multiple cases where parties are litigating open source licenses as contracts rather than as the IP / copyright licenses they were written to be. Contract theories let a plaintiff sidestep the questions copyright forces you to answer. 'Do you own the work? Is it protectable expression? Was it actually copied?'" He added: "Those questions are the foundation on which licenses are built. Open source licenses are grants of permission to use someone's intellectual property. If a case can't show that any intellectual property was owned or infringed, it's fair to ask whether enforcing the license as a bare contract supports open source licensing or quietly turns it into something else." With AI in the mix, this issue will eventually become one of those nasty IP matters developers hate, businesses want to avoid, but that courts must settle with expensive lawyers whose hourly rates worry even AI millionaires. After all, IP uncertainty isn't a minor paperwork issue. It is a supply-chain security and compliance problem. If you use AI-generated code, you may be importing unknown legal obligations into your software. If you are an open-source developer, your work may be used to improve a proprietary service that returns code without provenance, attribution, or meaningful reciprocity. And if you are a customer, you may be relying on software whose origins no one can fully explain. The Ninth Circuit ruling didn't solve any of that. We're in for a lot more open source litigation that will make SCO vs. the known Linux universe look like a kerfuffle over a parking ticket. Then there is the latest wrinkle: A federal antitrust lawsuit against Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI, and Google. The plaintiffs allege the companies coordinated to slow the development of advanced AI systems. The lawsuit points to public statements from AI leaders all calling for coordination to “pace” frontier AI development over a single weekend. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has argued for industry-wide coordination to slow frontier development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk have also publicly expressed versions of the view that powerful AI systems need controls and careful deployment. On its face, that sounds sensible. AI safety is a real issue. Anyone who says otherwise has not been paying attention. But there's a huge difference between all big AI players agreeing among themselves on how quickly a market should develop. This looks like an awful lot like competitors deciding who gets to compete, what they get to build, and when they may build it. The Big AI companies all look like good guys while simultaneously strangling their smaller competitors. To mere mortals, this may sound like an open-and-shut case. It's not. Antitrust law requires evidence of an agreement and actual harm to competition; executives making similar public comments is not enough. The plaintiffs will need considerably more than quotes about AI safety or responsible development to win. Besides, if they do win, so what? What recently looked like huge antitrust wins has had its teeth pulled when it came to actually punishing the likes of Google and its ad business, or its earlier "lose the case, win the settlement" with Google Search. Do you see the pattern here? Big AI has effectively argued that copyright law, open source licenses, and competition rules shouldn't slow them down. When creators object, they are told that training is fair use. When developers object, they are told that generated code is new code. When competitors object, they are told security requires the largest companies to coordinate. Funny how the answer always seems to leave Big AI with the data, the market, and the money, isn't it? The central issue isn't whether AI should be allowed to develop. It will develop. The issue is whether the companies building it should be allowed to treat everyone else’s work as a free raw-material supply, then use the resulting products to take away the creators’ traffic, revenue, and bargaining power. Unless we stop Big AI now from this land grab with GPUs, only a handful of trillionaires will really benefit from AI, with the rest of us becoming serfs in a 21st-century post-technology feudal system. ®

bc26475675090572: From Jamaluddin Aziz
Mara chairman Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki's call to end or restrict movies and dramas depicting bullying represents a familiar, knee-jerk reaction to deep-seated societal issues.

It is clear that while the anxiety surrounding youth violence in schools is entirely valid, the proposed censorship and blanket ban on creative narratives rest on an archaic understanding of how the media operates.
As media scholars, we have seen this script play out for over a century, and history has repeatedly proven that smashing the mirror does not cure the reflection.
To understand why this approach is fundamentally flawed, we must trace this anxiety back to the birth of media effects research in the early 20th century.
During the 1920s and 1930s, early theorists propagated what became known as the "Magic Bullet Theory" or the "Hypodermic Needle Theory".

This paradigm assumed that media messages were injected directly into a passive, helpless audience, immediately altering their behaviour and thoughts. It presumed that if a viewer saw violence on screen, they would inevitably replicate it on the streets.

By the 1940s, empirical research had thoroughly discredited this theory. Audiences are not a monolith, nor are they mindless vessels waiting to be programmed. Yet, the tradition of using the media as a convenient scapegoat for complex societal ills persists.

From comic books and rock music to video games and local cinema, authority figures have long favoured moral panics over structural analysis because blaming a screen is far easier than fixing a broken social fabric.

Crucially, the rapid evolution of media technology has completely transformed what it means to be an "audience". The very concept of "mass media" belonged to a bygone era of a one-to-many communication flow, a single broadcasting station transmitting to an uncritical mass. Today, that dynamic is dead.

The contemporary media landscape is highly decentralised and personalised. We no longer have passive consumers; we have "producers" who are individuals who simultaneously consume, critique, remix, and actively create content.
Modern audiences possess a sharp consciousness of their own individuality and exercise significant agency in how they interpret media.
Therefore, trying to eradicate bullying by banning a movie is a remarkably lazy policy response. It assumes a direct causal link that simply does not exist in a vacuum.

If the core fear is that a gullible audience will immediately mimic cinematic slang and adopt aggressive personas, we must look at the wider cultural landscape. Consider how the term "bossku" was enthusiastically adopted and chanted by political fans across the nation.

That phrase did not gain cultural dominance because of a movie script; it thrived because of real-world political dynamics, digital echo chambers, and active audience participation. Media does not dictate culture; it interacts with it.

To truly make sense of bullying and the bully, we must look beyond the screen. Banning stories about bullying only sanitises our media environment while leaving the actual victims unprotected in the real world.

We need to understand why bullying takes place, the psychological mechanisms behind peer pressure, and the systemic failures within our educational and familial institutions that allow aggression to go unchecked. To achieve this, we need rigorous data, not reactionary censorship.

I urge our relevant government agencies as well as the education; higher education; women, family and community development; and communications ministries to collaborate and offer substantial research grants dedicated to qualitative studies on youth deviance and bullying.
We must talk to the perpetrators, the victims, and the bystanders.

Only by conducting deep, qualitative research can we understand how bullies make sense of their own behaviour, how they rationalise their actions, and how subcultures form. Censorship is a temporary curtain; empirical understanding is the only real cure.
Let's stop blaming the filmmakers and start funding the solutions.
Jamaluddin Aziz is an associate professor in critical media studies at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia's Centre for Research in Media and Communication and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
